record.original_question: Let K ⊂ C be compact and let x0 ∈ K be a non-peak point for R(K), the uniform limits on K of rational functions with poles outside K. Will there always exist a continuous curve Γ in K terminating at x0 ? It is easy to see that if P∞ n −n−1 ≤ |z − x | ≤ 2−n }, and M n=1 2 M1 (An (x0 ) \ K) < ∞, where An (x0 ) = {z : 2 0 1 denotes 1-dimensional Hausdorff content, then Γ can be chosen to be a straight line segment. In this case, Øksendal [615] showed that the integrated Brownian motion starting at x0 stays inside K for a positive period of time, almost surely. There is an example of a compact set K and a non-peak point x0 ∈ K such that no straight line segment terminating at x0 is included in K. (B. Øksendal)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $K \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a compact set, and let $R(K)$ denote the uniform closure on $K$ of the algebra of rational functions with poles off $K$ (so $R(K)$ is a uniform algebra on $K$). A point $x_0 \in K$ is called a peak point for $R(K)$ if there exists $f \in R(K)$ with $f(x_0)=1$ and $|f(z)|<1$ for every $z \in K \setminus \{x_0\}$; otherwise $x_0$ is called a non-peak point.

Question: Suppose $x_0 \in K$ is a non-peak point for $R(K)$. Must there exist a continuous curve $\Gamma \subset K$ (i.e., the image of a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to K$) that terminates at $x_0$ (i.e., with $\gamma(1)=x_0$ and $\gamma(t)\neq x_0$ for $t<1$, or equivalently a non-degenerate continuum in $K$ containing $x_0$)?

Background facts to be assumed (not to be proved): 
(a) Writing $A_n(x_0) = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : 2^{-n-1} \le |z-x_0| \le 2^{-n}\}$ and $M_1$ for $1$-dimensional Hausdorff content, if 
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{-n-1}\, M_1\bigl(A_n(x_0)\setminus K\bigr) < \infty,$$
then such a curve $\Gamma$ may even be chosen to be a straight line segment ending at $x_0$.
(b) There exists a compact $K$ and a non-peak point $x_0\in K$ for which no straight line segment terminating at $x_0$ is contained in $K$, so the answer for line segments in general is negative.

Decide whether the existence of a continuous curve in $K$ terminating at every non-peak point of $R(K)$ holds in general.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not turn up a published resolution of Øksendal's question on whether every non-peak point for $R(K)$ is the endpoint of a continuous curve lying in $K$. The problem appears in compiled lists of open problems in function theory and no definitive solution (positive or negative) was located.
